ann_79.text: Through this part, more daytime minutes (112 to 249) do nothing until about 217 minutes, then slightly raise the predicted chance of leaving steadily, but only if the customer has no voice-mail plan: from about 2% to about 4%, against below 1% either way with a plan.

For customers without a voice-mail plan, daytime minutes slightly add to it only once they rise above about 218 minutes (between 171 and 265 minutes for different customers), from about 2% to about 7% for the typical customer (on the training data only).

This part acts on 1033 of 4000 customers, 283 of whom left; for the typical one (in Alabama, with about 234 daytime minutes and no voice-mail plan) it slightly raises the chance from about 2% to about 6% (on the training data only).
For that customer, a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it from about 6% to about 2%.

Across the usual range, more daytime minutes do nothing until about 218 minutes (between 171 minutes and 265 minutes for different customers), then slightly raise it steadily, to about 4% (on the training data only).
A higher daytime charge slightly raises it in an uneven way across customers, to about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_80.text: Through this part, the daytime charge clearly adds to the predicted chance of leaving only once it rises above about 41.59 US dollars (between 34.11 and 46.36 US dollars for different customers), and above that point in an uneven way across customers: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 2% to about 8%.

A higher evening charge (11.76 to 22.57 US dollars) does nothing until about 20.56 US dollars, then slightly raises it steadily, but only if the daytime charge is above 30.69 US dollars: from about 2% to about 5%, against about 2% either way otherwise.
Across the usual range, a higher daytime charge and a higher evening charge slightly raise it, both in an uneven way across customers, to about 2% to 3%.

Voice-mail messages slightly raise it steadily up to about 20 messages (between 9 and 28 messages for different customers), then no further, from about 2% to about 4% for the typical customer (on the training data only).

More international minutes (7 to 14) slightly lower it in an uneven way across customers, from about 3% to about 2%, and for a typical customer in Virginia they slightly lower it once they rise above about 3 minutes, from about 4% to about 2% (on the training data only).
Being in Alabama slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_81.text: Through this part, customer-service calls clearly add to the predicted chance of leaving from 3 calls upwards (between 1 and 3 calls for different customers), in an uneven way across customers: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 2% to about 13%.

For the typical customer this part acts on (one with 3 customer-service calls and about 166 daytime minutes), a higher daytime charge clearly lowers it steadily up to about 15.64 US dollars (between 7.93 and 31.04 US dollars for different customers), then no further: from about 11% at 19.07 US dollars to about 2% at 42.40 US dollars.

Customer-service calls slightly raise it, slowly at first, then faster, and even more so if the daytime charge is 30.69 US dollars or less: going from 0 to 3 calls moves it from about 2% to about 6%, against about 2% either way above that charge.
Across all customers, going from 0 to 3 calls slightly raises it in an uneven way, from about 2% to about 3%.
This part acts on 1303 of 4000 customers, 302 of whom left; for the typical one it slightly raises the chance from about 2% to about 3%.
An international plan slightly raises it and being in South Dakota slightly lowers it through this part (on the training data only).

ann_82.text: Through this part, being in Utah, Iowa or Arkansas slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving to about 2% to 3%, and North Dakota and New Mexico slightly lower it, staying at about 2% (on the training data only).
More voice-mail messages barely change it, slightly raising it while it stays at about 2% (on the training data only).

ann_83.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 2% to about 24%.
More voice-mail messages raise it quickly at first, then level off: from about 2% at 0 messages to about 10% at 32 messages (on the training data only).
California and Washington, compared with the states the model does not single out, raise it to about 9% and 7% (on the training data only).

New Jersey and Texas slightly raise it to about 4% to 5% and New York, Utah, Minnesota, Ohio, Oregon, Arizona, Indiana, Iowa and Arkansas to about 2% to 3%, while Vermont slightly lowers it to below 1% and Alaska, Wyoming, Illinois, Wisconsin, Nebraska, Missouri, North Dakota, Alabama, New Mexico and South Dakota to about 1% to 2% (on the training data only).
A voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%.
Three customer-service calls rather than none and a higher evening charge slightly raise it, both in an uneven way across customers, to about 2% to 3%.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance of leaving only slightly (on the training data only): more daytime minutes (112 to 249) do nothing until about 217 minutes, then raise it steadily, to about 4% at 249 minutes; more evening minutes, a higher night-time charge and a longer account each raise it steadily, to about 3%; more international minutes raise it in an uneven way, to about 3%; more evening calls lower it in an uneven way; and an area code other than 415 lowers it, staying at about 2%.
It ignores daytime calls, international calls, international charge, night-time calls and night-time minutes.

ann_79.original: HYPOTHESIS: two ReLU hinges on daytime usage that raise churn for heavy day users, mainly those without a voice-mail plan. total_day_minutes and total_day_charge are identical after z-scoring (max diff 5e-4), so the leaf uses both interchangeably. 1254 = relu(0.42*day - 0.73): on for day z > 1.74 (164 rows, churn 62% vs 12%), logit +2.08 per unit (up to +1.26). 3460 = relu(0.86*day - 0.83*voice_mail_plan - 0.85): on for day z > 0.39 without a voice-mail plan, z > 2.5 with one (995 rows, churn 28% vs 9.5%), logit +2.25 per unit (up to +5.3). EVIDENCE (train, n=4000): closed form above (max err 0.002); sensitivity: 3460 driven by voice_mail_plan (0.21) and day (0.21 total). summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 24%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 2%).

The model treats a higher voice-mail messages as raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves quickly at first, then levelling off: for a typical customer, it goes from about 2% at 0 messages to about 10% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower (on the training data only).

For a typical customer, the model gives a higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in California (about 9%) than if state is something other than Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Arkansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, North Dakota, Nebraska, Arizona, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, California, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, Wyoming (about 2%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, the customer-service calls only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from 3 calls (between 1 calls and 3 calls for different customers) upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 calls to 4 calls moves it from about 2% to about 13%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

Through one part of the model, total daytime charge only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 41.59 US dollars (between 34.11 US dollars and 46.36 US dollars for different customers): for a typical such customer, going from 0.00 US dollars to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 2% to about 8%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.
The model ignores total daytime calls, total international calls, total international charge, total night-time calls and total night-time minutes.
